title: Washed
summary_theology: A celebration of being made clean by Jesus. It joins two biblical pictures of cleansing, the blood of the cross that forgives sin and the washing that signs new life, and treats shame as something Christ has already carried and defeated (Revelation 1:5; 1 John 1:7-9; Colossians 2:13-14).
practical_worship_leadership: Works as the congregation's response after a prayer of confession and assurance of pardon, on baptism Sundays, and as an opener in youth and young-adult gatherings. In a multigenerational room, place it after a slower song about the cross so the celebration has something to answer, and give one sentence of setup so the energy stays tied to the gospel.
arrangement_tips:
Try clean, bright guitar parts that leave space for each other, with drums locked to a click so the room can find the pulse. Consider holding harmonies to one or two parts until the final passes so the words stay clear.

Before Sunday, test the key with the person leading and with a few untrained voices; a key that suits a youth band may sit too high for a mixed-age room. On a confession or baptism Sunday, consider reading Psalm 51:7 or 1 John 1:9 over a held chord before the downbeat.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Washed" means

"Washed" is a song about being made clean by Jesus. It celebrates the forgiveness won at the cross and sings about shame as something Christ has already dealt with, so a believer no longer has to carry it. This page covers the original recording by Elevation Rhythm, released as a single on Elevation Worship Records in 2025 and written by Mitch Wong, Joshua Holiday, Joe L. Barnes and Steven Furtick. Holiday has described its message as being made clean through the cross, set to a bright guitar-pop sound. That pairing of a weighty subject with a joyful feel is the best way into the song.

Two biblical pictures of cleansing run through it. The blood points to the cross, where 1 John 1:7 says the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin. The water echoes the washing language the New Testament uses for new life in Christ, as in Titus 3:5. Together they describe a forgiveness that is finished and a person who has been made new.

The sections below look at what that celebration does in a room and how to lead it with care.

## What this song does in a room

Picture a student who walks into youth group on a Wednesday night after a week they would rather nobody knew about. They stand near the back, arms folded, sure that everyone else in the room is cleaner than they are. A bright, fast song about being washed can sound at first like it belongs to someone else. Then the room starts singing about shame being taken away, and for that student it may be the first time forgiveness has been announced with joy instead of a lecture.

That is what a song like this offers. It gives a congregation a way to celebrate forgiveness out loud and together. Your church should keep its solemn songs about the cross, and it also needs a way to rejoice in what the cross accomplished. The risk is that energy outpaces understanding, and a room jumps for four minutes without connecting the joy to its reason. One sentence of setup, or a verse read before the downbeat, usually closes that gap.

## What this song is saying about God

The song makes a claim about what God has done with sin and with shame. Sin brings a guilt that stands between people and God. Shame is the fear that you are what you did. The gospel answers both. Colossians 2:13-14 says God forgave all trespasses and took the record of debt that stood against us out of the way, nailing it to the cross. Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross and despised the shame, treating it as something with no final claim on him.

That makes the song's joy a theological statement. The celebration rests on an accomplished event and on a promise that keeps applying it, since 1 John 1:9 tells believers that confession meets a God who is faithful to forgive and cleanse. For the person who keeps returning to the same failure, the cleansing has not run out.

The water imagery deserves a careful word. Churches understand baptism differently, and the song does not settle those debates. What every tradition can affirm with it is that the cleansing comes from Christ, and that water in Scripture signs the new life he gives.

## Scriptural backbone

Revelation 1:5 is the clearest single verse for this song. It praises Jesus as the one "that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood." 1 John 1:7 adds that "the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin," and verse 9 promises that God "is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

For the water, Ezekiel 36:25-26 has God promising to "sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean," followed by the gift of a new heart. Titus 3:5 says God saved us "by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost." Psalm 51:7 is the prayer underneath it all: "wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow." If you have time for one reading, Psalm 51:1-12 lets the room confess before it celebrates.

## How to use it in a service

Try it as the response after a prayer of confession. Many churches follow confession with an assurance of pardon; read 1 John 1:9 and let this song be the congregation's answer. It also suits baptism Sundays, when the water is already in front of everyone, and the weeks after Easter, while a church is still rejoicing in the resurrection.

In a youth or young-adult gathering it can open the night, since the energy invites people in quickly. In a multigenerational room, consider placing it second or third, after a slower song that sets the cross in front of people, so the celebration has something to answer. Avoid stacking it beside two or three other high-energy songs with a similar feel, which can blur the message into general excitement.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch for the person the song has not reached yet. Someone in your room has heard "you are forgiven" many times and still doubts it applies to them. A short line from you, inviting anyone who is unsure to sing it as a prayer, gives that person a way in.

Watch the speed. A bright song can rush words past a congregation that is still learning them. Rehearse at the tempo your room can sing, and let the band find its energy in dynamics.

Check the range. Sing it with a few untrained voices before Sunday and listen for strain at the top. In a mixed-age room, the key that suits a youth band may leave older voices behind.

Mind your own tradition's reading of the water. Whether your church baptizes infants, believers or both, a one-sentence frame keeps the song from being heard as a statement it does not make.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Guitarists, consider bright, clean tones and parts that leave space for each other; two guitars strumming the same rhythm will muddy a song that depends on clarity. Drummers, try locking to a click so the pulse stays steady and the room can find it. Bass players, sit with the kick and keep the lines simple so the low end stays clean under a busy top.

Vocalists, keep the lead clear on the words, since the message carries the song, and hold harmonies to one or two parts until the final passes. Techs, keep the lead vocal on top of a full mix. If the room is singing well at the end, ride the congregation mics up so the band can hear them, and keep the lighting warm and bright for a song of joy.

title: In The Presence Of The King
summary_theology: A Christmas worship song that brings the congregation before Jesus as King, joining the wonder of his birth to worship of his majesty. It stands in the line of the wise men who found the child and worshipped him (Matthew 2:11) and of Isaiah's promise that the child born to us will reign (Isaiah 9:6-7).
practical_worship_leadership: Introduce it early in Advent so regular attenders know it before Christmas Eve, then use it as the response after a nativity reading and again on Epiphany Sunday. Pair it with a familiar carol for guests, and frame any language of God's presence as a response to the King who has already come near in Christ.
arrangement_tips:
Try a warm piano bed with a soft pad, adding seasonal strings, brass or choir only on later passes so the song grows. Consider light drums with brushes or mallets early and a fuller groove only once the room is clearly singing.

Before Sunday, test the key with your leader and a few untrained voices. Decide in advance how many times to repeat any section and rehearse a clear ending, since an arrangement drawn from a live recording may run longer than your service order allows.
editorial_markdown:
## What "In The Presence Of The King" means

"In The Presence Of The King" is a Christmas worship song about coming before Jesus as King. It joins the wonder of his birth to worship of his majesty, so the manger and the throne belong to the same person. This page covers Charity Gayle's recording, a live-recorded single released ahead of her Christmas album His Name Shall Be, which pairs new songs with carols such as "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing." Gayle wrote it with Kyle Lee, Mitch Wong, Ryan Kennedy and Melanie Slay.

A fitting scriptural frame is the visit of the wise men in Matthew 2. They arrive asking for the one born King of the Jews, and when they find the child they fall down and worship him. Singing this song, a church can join them and worship the child as King.

Because it is a newer song, many congregations will meet it for the first time in Advent. The sections below look at how its worship works in a room during the Christmas season and how to lead it well.

## What this song does in a room

It is the second Sunday of Advent. The tree is up in the lobby, the children's program is two weeks away, and half the room is already tired from the season. Christmas songs can slide into nostalgia here: warm, familiar and easy to sing without thinking about who was born. A song that brings people before the King pushes against that drift. It asks a room to look at the nativity and respond the way the wise men did.

For guests, Christmas is often the one service they attend all year. A song centered on Jesus himself, more than on the atmosphere of the season, gives them a clear picture of why the church gathers at all. For long-time members, it can restore some wonder to a story they know too well.

Most rooms will need time with an unfamiliar song. Expect the first week to be more listening than singing, and plan the season around that.

## What this song is saying about God

The central claim is that the child in Bethlehem is the King. That is the Christmas confession of the New Testament. The angel tells Mary that her son will receive the throne of David and reign forever (Luke 1:32-33). Isaiah 9:6-7 names the child and places the government on his shoulder. Hebrews 1:6 says that when God brought his firstborn into the world, he called the angels to worship him.

That gives Christmas worship its weight. The incarnation is God himself coming near, and the fitting response to a King who comes near is to bow. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and his people beheld his glory.

The language of presence needs a careful word. Your music does not produce the presence of God. In Christ, God has already come to his people, and Jesus promises to be with them when they gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). Frame the song as a response to a King who has come, and the room will hear it rightly.

## Scriptural backbone

Matthew 2:1-11 is the story to read. The wise men ask, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews?" and when they find the child they "fell down, and worshipped him." Luke 2:8-20 gives the shepherds' side: the angel announces "a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord," and the shepherds return "glorifying and praising God."

Isaiah 9:6 supplies the names: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder." Psalm 24:7-10 asks, "Who is this King of glory?" and answers with the Lord himself. Philippians 2:6-11 traces the whole movement from manger to throne, ending with every knee bowing. If you read one passage before the song, read Matthew 2:9-11 slowly and let the room picture that moment of worship.

## How to use it in a service

Use it through Advent and Christmas, and consider bringing it back on Epiphany Sunday, when the wise men's story is the natural text. It works as a response after the Christmas Eve reading of Luke 2, or as the moment of worship after a nativity reading in a family service.

Pair it with a familiar carol so guests have something they know. A pattern that works in many rooms is a well-known carol, a scripture reading, then this song. If your church closes Christmas Eve with candles and "Silent Night," keep that tradition and place this song earlier in the order.

If you introduce it in Advent, sing it two or three weeks in a row before Christmas Eve so your regular attenders can carry it when the guests arrive.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch the calendar. A song released close to the season has little time to become familiar, and Christmas Eve is a hard night to teach a congregation something new. Introduce it early in Advent or save it for the following year.

Watch the length. Decide before Sunday how many times you will repeat any section and plan a clear ending, so the song does not outlast the room's attention on a crowded service night.

Watch the guests. Some people in your room at Christmas do not yet believe Jesus is a king. Invite instead of pressing. You might tell them they are welcome to listen while the church sings what it believes.

Check the range with a few untrained voices before you settle on a key, and remember that Christmas crowds include many people who rarely sing in public.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Keys players, consider a warm piano bed with a soft pad underneath, which suits the season and leaves room for the vocals. If your church adds strings, brass or a choir for Christmas, try saving those textures for later passes so the song grows. Drummers, consider light time with brushes or mallets early and a fuller groove only once the room is clearly singing.

Vocalists, a small team singing the melody in unison before splitting into harmony helps a congregation learn it. Techs, Christmas services bring guest musicians and extra inputs, so label channels clearly and walk through every transition in rehearsal. Keep lyric slides a line ahead, since many people in the room will be reading every word.

title: It Really Is Amazing Grace
summary_theology: A celebration of salvation by grace that keeps John Newton's hymn verses and answers them with a new chorus and bridge. It confesses that God saves people who could not save themselves, by grace through faith, and turns that confession into thanksgiving (Ephesians 2:1-10).
practical_worship_leadership: A strong bridge between generations: older members carry Newton's verses with confidence and younger members carry the new sections with energy. Use it as an opener on a celebration Sunday, as a response after preaching on grace, or around baptisms and testimonies. Choose one recording for your team and teach it consistently.
arrangement_tips:
Consider giving Newton's verses a hymn-like setting, with piano or acoustic guitar and light drums, then opening into the full band for the new chorus so the shift is clear. If you have a choir or a larger vocal team, try bringing them in on the later choruses.

The Phil Wickham and Crowder single and the Passion live version are separate recordings; pick one as your team's reference and do not mix their structures. Before Sunday, sing both the hymn verses and the new chorus with a few untrained voices to choose a key that serves both.
editorial_markdown:
## What "It Really Is Amazing Grace" means

"It Really Is Amazing Grace" is a celebration of salvation by grace. It keeps John Newton's familiar hymn verses and adds a new chorus and bridge that answer them with joy, so the church affirms that the old hymn's claims about grace are still true. This page covers the studio single by Phil Wickham and Crowder, released in early 2026 with a choir on the recording. The new material is credited to Phil Wickham, Jonathan Smith and David Crowder, and Crowder also led the song at Passion 2026, so your team may hear a Passion live version as well.

It is a different song from Wickham's earlier "This Is Amazing Grace" and from Chris Tomlin's "Amazing Grace (My Chains Are Gone)," which builds on the same hymn with its own chorus. Wickham has said the song reminds him how deeply he needs God's forgiveness and grace, and Crowder has spoken of the wonder of being rescued and redeemed.

Ephesians 2:1-10 supplies the frame: dead in sin, made alive by God's mercy, saved by grace through faith. The sections below follow that frame into a Sunday service.

## What this song does in a room

Watch an older woman in the fourth row when the band starts the first verse. She has sung these words at funerals and at baptisms, and she knows them without looking at the screen. Then the new chorus arrives, louder and brighter, and she has a choice. She can fold her arms because the song changed, or she can join a younger generation celebrating the same grace she has trusted for decades.

That moment is the opportunity in this song. Multigenerational churches rarely get a place where both groups can stand inside one hymn. The familiar verses give older members confidence, and the new sections give younger members a way to answer them with energy.

It can go wrong in either direction. If the band treats the verses as a warm-up before the real song, the people who love Newton feel dismissed. If the band holds back when the new chorus arrives, the celebration never comes. Give each part its due.

## What this song is saying about God

The theology is the theology of the hymn it builds on: salvation is God's work from start to finish. Newton, a former slave-ship captain, wrote out of his own experience of undeserved mercy, and the hymn has carried that confession for generations. Grace reaches people who could not reach God and gives what they could never earn.

Ephesians 2 states it plainly. People were dead in trespasses, and God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. Paul then guards the point: salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, so that no one can boast. Paul calls himself the chief of sinners in 1 Timothy 1:15 and says his own rescue is a pattern for everyone who will believe.

The new sections add the response that grace produces. Thanksgiving, freedom and testimony follow from being found. A congregation singing them is doing what Ephesians 2:10 describes, living as God's workmanship, and joy is part of that life.

## Scriptural backbone

Ephesians 2:4-5 is the heart of it: "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved)." Verses 8-9 complete the thought: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast."

Newton's best-known lines echo two Gospel scenes. In Luke 15:24 the father says of the prodigal son that he "was lost, and is found." In John 9:25 the healed man answers his questioners, "whereas I was blind, now I see." 1 Timothy 1:15 gives Paul's own testimony that "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." If you read one passage before the song, read Ephesians 2:1-10 straight through.

## How to use it in a service

It works as an opener on a celebration Sunday, when you want the room on its feet from the first song and grounded in something it already knows. It also serves as a response after a sermon on grace, conversion or the prodigal son, and it fits naturally around baptisms and testimonies. Consider placing a short testimony of grace just before it and beginning the first verse quietly under the last sentence.

Do not sing it in the same set as another arrangement of Amazing Grace. Two versions of the same verses in one service blur together. If your church already sings "My Chains Are Gone," decide which version you will use for a season.

The Wickham and Crowder single and the Passion live recording are separate versions, so choose one for your team and teach it consistently.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch the wording of the verses. Hymnals and recordings vary slightly in Newton's text, and older members may sing the version they learned as children. Put the words you are using on the screen and expect a few voices to differ.

Watch the handoff from hymn to chorus. The change of energy is the point of the song, and it needs to be clear. A count-off, a drum fill or a simple raised hand can tell the room something new is starting.

Check the range. The hymn verses and the new chorus may not sit in the same comfortable zone for your congregation, so test both with a few untrained voices before choosing a key.

Watch for repetition in the new sections. Decide in advance how many times you will sing them.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Keys players, consider a hymn-like piano setting for Newton's verses, with clear voicings that an older congregation recognizes. Drummers, try staying light or out through the first verse and arriving fully on the new chorus so the shift is unmistakable. Bass players, hold roots under the verses and add movement once the band opens up.

Vocalists, if you have a choir or a larger vocal team, bring them in on the later choruses; the recording leans on a choir, and a congregation hears that support as permission to sing louder. Techs, build separate scenes or snapshots for the hymn verses and the full-band sections, and make sure the lyric operator knows which version of the verses you are using.

title: There's Nothing That Our God Can't Do
summary_theology: A declaration that nothing is impossible for God, rooted in Luke 1:37, Matthew 19:26 and Job 42:2. Scripture always ties God's power to his wisdom and goodness, so the song is best sung as trust in God's sovereign will, not as a promise of any particular outcome.
practical_worship_leadership: Use it as a call to worship, after preaching on faith or prayer, or on missions Sundays. Pair it with an honest song of waiting so grieving people are not left out, and keep spoken exhortations within what Scripture actually promises.
arrangement_tips:
Consider a steady groove with the build carried by dynamics, not tempo, and a sustained pad under quieter passes. If the song leads into prayer, plan a clean transition so sound and lyrics stay present while people respond.

Test the key with your leader and a few untrained voices before Sunday, and decide how many times to repeat any section. If your church first learned another recording, compare its structure with the Passion version before teaching it.
editorial_markdown:
## What "There's Nothing That Our God Can't Do" means

"There's Nothing That Our God Can't Do" is a declaration of God's power. It calls a congregation to praise God as the one for whom nothing is impossible, and to trust him with whatever they are facing. This page covers the live recording by Passion with Kristian Stanfill, released as a single in December 2019 on sixstepsrecords and Sparrow Records. Stanfill wrote it with Brandon Lake and Jonathan Smith. Other artists have since recorded it, including Women Who Worship and Evan Craft, so your congregation may have met it in more than one form.

The scriptural frame is the angel's word to Mary in Luke 1:37, that with God nothing shall be impossible, and Job's confession in Job 42:2 that God can do everything. Both texts hold power and purpose together. God can do anything, and what he does is always wise and good.

That balance is the key to leading the song well, and the sections below keep returning to it.

## What this song does in a room

You start the song, and a man near the front whose wife began chemotherapy on Tuesday sings louder than anyone around him. A few rows behind him, a woman who buried her son last spring stops singing. They heard the same title, and it landed in two different places.

A song that declares God's power will always meet both people, and leading it well means holding them together. For the first, the song is fuel for faith and prayer. For the second, it can sound like an accusation, as if her son died because someone did not believe enough. Your framing decides which song the room hears.

Framed as praise of who God is, the song does real good. The claim is simple enough for a room to catch quickly, and it lifts people's eyes from their circumstances to God. As a call to worship, it reminds a tired congregation that the God they gathered to meet is not small.

## What this song is saying about God

The song claims that God is all-powerful, and Scripture agrees without hesitation. What Scripture never does is separate that power from God's wisdom and goodness, and each text behind this song shows the connection.

In Luke 1, the angel tells Mary that nothing is impossible with God, and Mary answers by surrendering herself to God's word. Her response is trust. In Matthew 19:26, Jesus says that with God all things are possible while answering a question about who can be saved; the impossible thing God does there is rescue people from sin. In Job 42:2, Job confesses that God can do everything after a season of loss God never fully explained to him.

So the song's confidence is confidence in God's sovereignty. God can do anything, and he will do what is good. Sometimes that means healing or rescue. Sometimes, as Paul learned in 2 Corinthians 12, it means grace sufficient to carry what God chooses not to remove. Both come from the same powerful God.

## Scriptural backbone

Luke 1:37 is the root: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." Read it with the next verse, where Mary answers, "be it unto me according to thy word." Matthew 19:26 records Jesus saying, "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible." Job 42:2 gives Job's confession: "I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee."

Daniel 3:17-18 is a useful companion text. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego tell the king that their God "is able to deliver us," and then add, "But if not," they still will not bow. That is the posture this song needs: full confidence in God's power and full surrender to his will. Ephesians 3:20 closes the circle by praising God as the one who "is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think."

## How to use it in a service

The song works well as a call to worship or early in a set, when you want to turn a room's attention to God's greatness. It also fits after a sermon on faith, prayer or the promises of God, and on missions Sundays, when a church is reminded that no place or people is beyond God's reach.

Consider pairing it with an honest song of waiting or lament, before or after. That pairing tells the congregation that declaring God's power and grieving unanswered prayer belong in the same church.

Use care at prayer-ministry nights and healing services. The song can carry a time of prayer for the sick, as long as your words around it trust God's will and stop short of promising outcomes.

Avoid using it to rally a room around a building campaign or a budget target. The song is about God, and attaching it to an institutional goal shrinks it.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch your spoken words more than the song. The most common misstep is an exhortation between choruses that promises more than Scripture does, such as telling the room that everyone who believes will be healed this week. Speak about God's ability and God's goodness, and leave the outcomes with him.

Watch for the person who stops singing. If someone goes quiet, it may be grief, not unbelief. A sentence from the front, saying that this song is true even on days we cannot see it, keeps the door open for them.

Check the range with a few untrained voices before Sunday, and decide in advance how many times you will repeat any section. Declaration songs can run long when a band is enjoying them, and a congregation tires faster than a stage does.

Watch which version your church learned. If people know the Women Who Worship recording, compare structures before you introduce the Passion form.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Drummers, consider a steady, confident groove and let dynamics carry the build; rushing a declaration song makes it sound anxious. Bass players, lock with the kick and keep the lines simple. Keys players, a sustained pad under the quieter sections gives the room a floor to stand on when the band pulls back.

Vocalists, keep the melody clear and the harmonies supportive, since a congregation needs to hear the tune before it can declare anything. Techs, if your church has congregation mics, ride them up on the final passes. If the song leads into a ministry time, prepare a clean transition so the screen and the sound do not drop out while people are still responding.

title: Hard Fought Hallelujah
summary_theology: A song of praise offered in struggle. It stands in the biblical tradition of worship in the dark, from Paul and Silas singing at midnight (Acts 16:25) to Habakkuk rejoicing when the fields fail, and treats praise as a response to God's nearness and faithfulness, offered in weakness, rather than an achievement of the worshipper.
practical_worship_leadership: Use it after preaching on suffering or perseverance, or as an honest call to worship in a heavy week. Read a psalm of lament such as Psalm 13 before it and follow it with a song of God's faithfulness so the room ends on God's character.
arrangement_tips:
Try opening sparse with one guitar or piano and adding the band gradually so the build feels earned. Consider sustained bass notes in the quieter sections, and leave dynamic room in the mix.

Brandon Lake's original single and the later version with Jelly Roll are different recordings; choose one as your team's reference. Test the key with your leader and a few untrained voices so the room can still sing at the emotional peak.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Hard Fought Hallelujah" means

"Hard Fought Hallelujah" is a song about praising God in the middle of struggle. It gives voice to someone who is wrestling with doubt and pain and chooses to worship anyway, trusting that God is faithful when feelings say otherwise. This page covers Brandon Lake's original recording, released as a single in November 2024 on Provident Label Group. Lake wrote it with Steven Furtick, Benjamin Hastings, Chris Brown and Rodrick Simmons. Lake later released a version with Jelly Roll, so some people in your room may know the song from that recording.

The title names the song's honesty. Some praise comes easily, and some has to be fought for through grief, fear or a long season of unanswered prayer. The song treats that second kind as worship too.

Its clearest biblical picture is Paul and Silas in Acts 16, beaten and locked in stocks, praying and singing to God at midnight. The sections below look at how that kind of praise works on a Sunday.

## What this song does in a room

Think about the people who walk in on a Sunday carrying something they have not told anyone. A marriage under strain. A child who has walked away from faith. A belief that feels thinner than it used to. Many worship songs assume a room that is already happy, and those people often stand through them in silence. This song gives them permission to bring the fight with them.

That honesty can change a room. When a congregation sings about praise that costs something, the people who are struggling discover they are not the only ones. The person beside them may be fighting too.

There is a second gift. People who are doing well that week learn something about their brothers and sisters. They are singing beside people for whom every word is costly, and that builds a solidarity that a celebration song alone cannot.

## What this song is saying about God

The song sits inside a long biblical tradition of worship offered in the dark. The Psalms are full of it. Psalm 34 begins with David resolving to bless the Lord at all times, and its heading ties the psalm to a season when he was running for his life. Habakkuk ends his book by rejoicing in God while the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield nothing.

The title invites one misreading worth naming. "Hard fought" can sound as though the worshipper earns something by pushing through, as if praise were an achievement of grit. Scripture frames it the other way. Praise in hard seasons is a response to God's faithfulness, offered in weakness. Psalm 145:18 says the Lord is near to all who call on him. God's nearness comes first, and praise answers it.

That is good news for the person who has no fight left. A weak hallelujah still counts, and God hears the one who can barely say it as clearly as the one who shouts it.

## Scriptural backbone

Acts 16:25 is the scene: "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." Verse 26 records the earthquake that opened the doors, but the singing came first, before any rescue was in sight. The listening prisoners are worth noticing too. Praise in the dark is a witness.

Psalm 34:1 gives the resolve: "I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth." Verse 4 gives the reason: "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears." Psalm 145:18 promises that "the LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him." Habakkuk 3:17-18 is the classic text for this kind of worship: though everything fails, "yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Hebrews 13:15 calls it "the sacrifice of praise."

## How to use it in a service

Use it after a sermon on suffering, perseverance or lament, when the room needs a way to respond that does not pretend. It also works as an honest call to worship in a heavy week, after a tragedy in your community or a loss in your church family, when starting with pure celebration would ring false.

Consider reading a psalm of lament before it. Psalm 13 is short and moves from "how long" to trust in six verses, which gives the song a frame. Afterward, move to a song of steady confidence in God's faithfulness so the room ends on God's character.

It also fits testimony moments. A short testimony from someone who kept worshipping through a hard season, told without a tidy ending, can set it up well.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch for performance. A song about costly praise can tempt a leader to dramatize the struggle from the stage. Keep your own delivery honest and let the congregation's experience carry the weight.

Watch the end of your set. If this song closes the service, people may leave holding the fight without the God who meets them in it. Make sure something after it speaks of God's faithfulness.

Watch the version. If your congregation knows the Jelly Roll recording, they may expect a different shape from the original. Choose one form for your team and stay with it.

Check the range before Sunday with a few untrained voices. Songs with a raw emotional peak can climb out of a congregation's reach, and you want people singing at that moment, not watching.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Band, think of the arrangement as a journey from struggle toward resolve. Try opening sparse, with a single guitar or piano, and let the full band arrive gradually so the build feels earned. Drummers, consider holding back early and committing fully only when the song reaches its strongest declarations. Bass players, sustained notes in the quieter sections leave room for the vocal to carry the emotion.

Vocalists, honesty matters more than polish here. A slightly raw lead can serve the song better than a perfect one, as long as the melody stays clear enough to follow. Techs, leave dynamic room in the mix so the build can grow, and avoid compressing the quiet sections up to the level of the loud ones.

title: How Great Is the Greatness of God
summary_theology: A modern hymn of praise to the triune God. It celebrates the faithfulness of the Father, the saving work of the Son at Calvary and the gift of the indwelling Spirit, and calls believers to give thanks for God's greatness in daily life and in trials (Psalm 36:5; Psalm 145:3; John 11:25-26).
practical_worship_leadership: Use it as an opening hymn, on Trinity Sunday, after preaching on God's attributes, or at funerals where John 11 is read. Introduce it several weeks in a row and let it sit beside classic hymns such as Holy, Holy, Holy or Great Is Thy Faithfulness.
arrangement_tips:
Consider a piano-led or acoustic setting with light percussion, leaving space for the congregation to carry the melody. If your church uses organ or choir, try them on the final verse.

Hymns like this are written for congregations, so a simple arrangement usually serves better than a busy one. Before Sunday, test the key with a few untrained voices and choose the one where the chorus sits comfortably for the whole room.
editorial_markdown:
## What "How Great Is the Greatness of God" means

"How Great Is the Greatness of God" is a hymn of praise to the triune God. It celebrates the faithfulness of the Father, the saving work of the Son at Calvary and the gift of the Spirit, and calls the church to give thanks for that greatness on ordinary days and hard ones. Matt Boswell, Matt Papa and Bryan Fowler wrote it. This page covers the live recording credited to Boswell, Fowler, Papa and Sing!, released as a single on the Getty Music label in 2024.

The title can cause confusion. This is a different song from Chris Tomlin's "How Great Is Our God" and from the older hymn "How Great Thou Art," though it sits comfortably beside both. Churches that already sing Boswell and Papa's "His Mercy Is More" will recognize the same commitment to clear, singable doctrine.

Psalm 36:5 sets the scale: God's mercy reaches to the heavens and his faithfulness to the clouds. John 11:25-26 adds the hope at the center, Jesus as the resurrection and the life. The sections below look at how a hymn like this serves a congregation and how to teach it.

## What this song does in a room

Hymn-loving churches often struggle to find new songs that feel at home beside the old ones. A congregation raised on "Great Is Thy Faithfulness" and "Holy, Holy, Holy" can be wary of anything written recently. This song gives those rooms something new with the doctrinal weight they expect from the old hymns, written for a congregation to sing together.

In contemporary rooms it does a different job. It slows a room down enough to think about who God is without draining the energy. Worshippers who have mostly sung about their own experience get a song that turns them outward, toward the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

The moment to watch for is when a congregation starts singing doctrine with joy. When that happens, people who think of theology as dry discover it can be sung at full voice.

## What this song is saying about God

The song is Trinitarian praise. It names the faithfulness of the Father, the saving work of the Son at Calvary and the Spirit given to live in believers. That is the shape of the gospel itself. The Father sends, the Son redeems, and the Spirit applies that redemption and sustains the people who receive it. Singing all three in one song teaches a congregation to worship the God the Bible reveals.

It also ties God's greatness to ordinary life. Greatness can sound distant, as if God were too large to care. The song brings it close, since the faithfulness that holds the universe also meets a believer in daily work and in the hardest days. John 11 shows how. Jesus speaks the words of verses 25-26 to Martha at her brother's tomb, before he raises Lazarus. His greatness arrives in the middle of grief.

That makes the song suitable for both celebration and sorrow. The same truths that lift a room on a bright Sunday steady it at a funeral.

## Scriptural backbone

Psalm 36:5 is the anchor: "Thy mercy, O LORD, is in the heavens; and thy faithfulness reacheth unto the clouds." Verse 7 follows with wonder: "How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God!" Psalm 145:3 states the theme of the title: "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable."

John 11:25-26 carries the hope: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die." 2 Corinthians 13:14 gives a Trinitarian blessing that pairs well with the song: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Lamentations 3:22-23 adds that God's compassions "are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

## How to use it in a service

It makes a strong opening hymn or call to worship, since it names who God is before the congregation asks anything of him. It fits Trinity Sunday naturally, and it serves well after a sermon on God's attributes or faithfulness.

Consider it for funerals and memorial services where John 11 is read. A congregation can sing it through tears, and the resurrection hope gives grieving families something solid.

Pair it with classic hymns of God's greatness on either side, or use it to end a service, followed by 2 Corinthians 13:14 as a benediction.

When you introduce it, plan three or four weeks in a row. Hymns earn their place through repetition, and a congregation needs a few Sundays before it sings the verses with confidence.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch the arrangement. A hymn like this is built for congregational voices, and a busy band can bury them. If people stop singing, pull instruments out before you push volume up.

Watch the title in your planning. Because it resembles "How Great Is Our God," make sure your planning software, slides and licensing reports point to the right song.

Check the range. Sing it with a few untrained voices before you choose a key, and listen for whether the chorus sits comfortably for the whole room.

Watch the pace of the verses. Doctrinally rich words need a little time to land, and rushing them turns theology into syllables.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Keys players, consider leading from the piano with full, hymn-style voicings that a congregation can follow. Guitarists, an acoustic rhythm part is usually enough; add electric only for color. Drummers, try light time or brushes on the verses and a fuller pattern on later choruses, always staying under the congregation. If your church has organ or choir, consider bringing them in on the final verse.

Vocalists, sing the melody clearly in unison on the first verse so people can learn it, then add simple harmony. Techs, mix this one as a congregational hymn: vocals and piano forward, band supportive, and congregation mics up if you have them, so the room can hear itself sing.

title: Count 'Em
summary_theology: A celebration of God's mighty works, from healing and restoration to deliverance and resurrection, that are too many to count. It roots those works in God's holiness (1 Samuel 2:2) and keeps the credit on him (Acts 3:12-16), while Scripture's own record reminds the church that faithful people also wait (Hebrews 11:39).
practical_worship_leadership: Use it on testimony and thanksgiving Sundays, or after preaching on the miracles of Jesus or the book of Acts. Invite people to remember what God has done, acknowledge those who are still waiting, and avoid promising specific healings.
arrangement_tips:
Consider confident, steady energy locked to a click, with rhythmic guitar parts that leave room for a lyric full of detail. Try group vocals on the recurring refrain so the congregation hears it as theirs to join.

Test the key with a few untrained voices and decide your repeats in advance. If testimonies follow the song, prepare a handheld mic and a clear slide so the transition is quick.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Count 'Em" means

"Count 'Em" is a celebration of God's mighty works. It names the kinds of things God has done, raising the dead, healing, restoring what was broken and setting captives free, and concludes that there are too many to count. Brandon Lake has called it his "bragging-on-God song," and that is the simplest way to understand it. This page covers Lake's original recording, released as a single in August 2023 on Provident Label Group and included on his album Coat of Many Colors. Lake wrote it with Jacob Sooter and Hank Bentley.

You may see the title written "Count Em'." It is a different song from the older hymn "Count Your Blessings," though both call people to remember what God has done and praise him for it.

Psalm 40:5 is the natural frame, where David says God's wonderful works are more than can be numbered. 1 Samuel 2:2 gives the reason they matter, since there is none holy like the Lord. The sections below look at how to lead a song that celebrates miracles without overpromising them.

## What this song does in a room

Some churches rarely hear testimony. People come, sing, listen and leave, and the stories of what God has done in their lives stay private. A song that piles up God's works gives a room a different habit. It trains people to remember out loud.

Picture the moment after the song when you ask, without pressure, whether anyone has seen God at work this year. A few hands go up. A grandmother mentions a grandson who is back in church. A man mentions a job that came through after months of waiting. None of the stories is dramatic, and every one belongs on the list.

The song also meets people who are waiting. Somewhere in the room is a person who has prayed for healing for years and has not received it. For that person, a song full of miracles can hurt. The way you frame it makes the difference between encouragement and burden.

## What this song is saying about God

The first claim is about God's character. The works the song celebrates flow from who God is. Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2 begins with God's holiness and only then describes how he lifts the poor and humbles the proud. God acts this way because he is holy, good and faithful.

The second claim concerns boasting. Scripture says some bragging is right. Psalm 34:2 says, "My soul shall make her boast in the LORD," and Paul writes that whoever glories should glory in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31). What matters is the direction of the boast. In Acts 3, after a lame man walks, Peter asks the crowd why they stare as if he and John had done it by their own power, and he gives the credit to the name of Jesus. A song that brags on God keeps the spotlight on him.

The third claim needs pastoral care. God has healed, delivered and even raised the dead, and he is still able to act in power. He has not promised that every sick person will be healed before the resurrection. Hebrews 11 lists people who saw great deliverance, then people who were mocked, imprisoned and killed, and says all of them were commended for their faith. Both lists belong in the count.

## Scriptural backbone

Psalm 40:5 speaks of God's wonderful works and his thoughts toward his people, and says, "if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered." 1 Samuel 2:2 grounds those works in God's character: "There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God."

Acts 3:16 shows where the credit goes after a miracle: "his name through faith in his name hath made this man strong, whom ye see and know." John 21:25 says that if everything Jesus did were written down, "even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." Hebrews 11:39 keeps the count honest: "these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise." If you read one passage before the song, Psalm 40:1-5 moves from waiting to testimony in a few verses.

## How to use it in a service

Use it on testimony Sundays, at the start of a service built around thanksgiving, or as a response after preaching on the miracles of Jesus or the book of Acts. It can also open a time of prayer for the sick, as long as the words around it trust God's will.

Consider pairing it with a time of remembering. Before the song, invite people to recall one thing God has done for them this year. Afterward, let two or three people share briefly.

On Thanksgiving weekend it can sit beside a classic hymn of gratitude, so older and younger members are counting together.

Avoid placing it straight after a lament or a time of grief. A sudden list of miracles can feel dismissive to people who are still in that moment. Put it later, after the room has been comforted.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch what you say about healing. Declare what God has done and what he is able to do, and avoid promising that everyone in the room will receive a particular miracle this week.

Watch for the person who is still waiting. A sentence acknowledging that some in the room are praying for things they have not yet seen gives them a place inside the song.

Watch the spotlight. A bragging song can drift toward the band or the leader. Keep your words and your posture pointing to God.

Plan your repeats and check the range. Decide in advance how many times you will repeat any section, and test the key with a few untrained voices.

Watch the title on your slides and in your planning software. With two spellings in circulation, it is easy to create duplicate entries.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Drummers and bass players, aim for confident energy, not frantic energy; lock to a click and let dynamics do the building. Electric players, consider rhythmic parts that leave room for the vocal, since the lyric moves through a long list of God's works and each line needs to be heard.

Vocalists, the lead should prioritize diction, because a list only lands if people catch each item. Consider group vocals on the recurring refrain so the congregation hears it as theirs to join. Techs, if you plan testimonies afterward, have a handheld mic ready and a clear slide on screen so the transition is quick and nobody waits in silence.

title: Just That Good
summary_theology: A song of grateful joy in the goodness of God. It finds joy in God's presence (Psalm 16:11) and measures his goodness by his grace, which is sufficient in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), not by how a particular week is going.
practical_worship_leadership: Use it as an opener, a sending song, on Thanksgiving weekend or in young-adult gatherings. Place a reading or song that acknowledges weakness before it so people carrying hard weeks can join, and tell the room why God is worth thanking instead of telling them how to feel.
arrangement_tips:
Try a steady, joyful groove locked to a click, leaving space in the verses and filling out the texture as the song builds. Keep harmonies simple so the melody stays clear for a congregation still learning it.

Test the key with a few untrained voices; a key that suits a young-adult room may sit high for an older congregation. If the room sings loudly at the end, bring the congregation mics up and ease the band back.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Just That Good" means

"Just That Good" is a song of grateful joy. It looks at the grace and mercy God has shown and answers with praise, because God is simply that good. Kristian Stanfill wrote it with Patrick Mayberry and Ethan Hulse. This page covers the live recording by Passion and Kristian Stanfill, the title track of Just That Good (Live From Passion 2026), released in March 2026 on sixstepsrecords and Capitol CMG. Stanfill also recorded the song on his earlier solo album Come To Jesus, so your team may already know that studio version. Passion's gatherings are built around college students, though the song's claim belongs to every generation.

Two scriptures frame it. Psalm 16:11 says that in God's presence is fullness of joy. 2 Corinthians 12:9 says his grace is sufficient and his strength is made perfect in weakness. Together they explain the song's joy. God's goodness is measured by his grace, and it holds when life does not.

The sections below look at how to lead that kind of joy in a real room.

## What this song does in a room

It is a Thursday night in October at a campus ministry. Midterms are close, a few students are homesick, and one of them just found out a parent lost a job. Then the band starts a song about how good God is. For some of those students it lands as relief. For others it lands as pressure to feel something they do not.

The difference often comes from what the room sees in the leader. If the joy on stage looks like a performance, tired people fold their arms. If it looks like gratitude from someone who has also been tired, they lean in.

When a room catches the song, gratitude spreads. People start remembering specific mercies, and some will respond visibly: hands raised, louder singing, a few people standing who were sitting. Let that happen without demanding it.

## What this song is saying about God

The song's claim is about God's goodness, and the Bible makes that claim everywhere. Psalm 34:8 invites people to taste and see that the Lord is good. Psalm 107:1 calls for thanks because his mercy endures forever. Goodness belongs to God's character, so it does not rise and fall with the week a congregation is having.

That is where the song needs care. In some rooms "God is good" has come to mean "my circumstances are good." Paul's testimony in 2 Corinthians 12 corrects that. He asked three times for relief and did not receive it. God's answer was his grace, and Paul ended up boasting in his weakness. Goodness in Scripture is measured by what God gives of himself.

Psalm 16 makes the same point from another angle. David calls the Lord his portion and his cup, and the joy he describes is joy in God's presence more than in anything God provides. A congregation singing this song is invited into that kind of joy.

## Scriptural backbone

Psalm 16:11 is the first anchor: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore." 2 Corinthians 12:9 is the second: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."

Psalm 34:8 gives the invitation: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Psalm 103:2 calls the soul to remember: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Psalm 107:1 gives the reason for thanks: "O give thanks unto the LORD, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever." If you read one passage before the song, read Psalm 103:1-5 and let the room hear a list of God's benefits before it sings about them.

## How to use it in a service

It works as an opener when you want a room to start with gratitude, and as a sending song at the end of a service. It fits Thanksgiving weekend, a Sunday with baptisms, and services that include testimony.

In college and young-adult ministries it can anchor a night of worship. In a multigenerational church, consider pairing it with an older hymn of God's goodness, such as "Great Is Thy Faithfulness," so the whole room has a way in.

Consider placing it after a song or reading that acknowledges weakness. When 2 Corinthians 12 or a short lament comes first, the joy of this song sounds earned, and people carrying hard weeks can join it.

If your team is learning several songs from the Passion 2026 album, consider teaching this one on its own first instead of alongside two or three other new tracks. A congregation learns one new melody at a time, and a song of thanks is easier to sing with conviction once the tune feels familiar. Bring it back the following week before you add the next new song.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch for forced joy. Telling a room how to feel rarely works. Tell them why God is worth thanking, and let the feeling follow.

Watch for the person whose week contradicts the song. A short line from you, saying that God's goodness holds even when circumstances do not look good, invites them in without asking them to pretend.

Plan the length. Celebration songs can stretch when the band is enjoying itself, and a congregation's energy fades sooner than the stage's. Decide your repeats in advance.

Check the range with a few untrained voices before Sunday. A key that suits a young-adult room may sit high for an older congregation.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Drummers, consider a steady, joyful groove locked to a click so the room can clap or move without the tempo drifting. Bass players, keep the low end simple and tight with the kick. Keys and guitar players, try leaving space in the verses and filling out the texture only as the song builds, so the celebration has room to grow.

If your band is small, try building the arrangement around one acoustic guitar or keys player who can carry the whole song alone, then add other parts only where they help the room sing. A song of thanks loses nothing when it stays simple, and a smaller sound often lets the congregation hear itself.

Vocalists, sing it like good news, and keep harmonies simple so the melody stays clear for a congregation that is still learning it. Techs, if the room starts singing loudly, bring the congregation mics up and ease the band back slightly in the final passes so people can hear one another.

title: Though War Break Out Against Me
summary_theology: A sung setting of the opening of Psalm 27. It confesses the Lord as light, salvation and stronghold, grounds courage in God's presence instead of the absence of threat, and centers on the desire to dwell with God and behold his beauty (Psalm 27:1-5).
practical_worship_leadership: Use it with Psalm 27 preaching, in seasons of crisis, or when praying for persecuted believers. Pair it with its sister song In The Land Of The Living or read the rest of the psalm, and keep the war language away from political or national enemies.
arrangement_tips:
Consider simple voicings that keep every word of the psalm clear, and build the band gradually toward the strongest declarations of confidence. Try a single voice on the first pass before adding harmonies.

Put the psalm reference on the opening slide. Test the key with a few untrained voices, and give the congregation several weeks to learn a Scripture text that may be wordier than a typical chorus.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Though War Break Out Against Me" means

"Though War Break Out Against Me" is a sung setting of Psalm 27. It takes David's confidence that the Lord is his light and his salvation and turns it into a song of trust for anyone facing opposition or fear. Brooke Ligertwood, a co-writer of "What A Beautiful Name" and "King of Kings," wrote it alone for EAT, her 2026 album built from the words of Scripture. The song covers the opening of the psalm, and its sister track on the album, "In The Land Of The Living," continues it, so the two can be sung as a pair.

The title comes from verse 3, where David says that even if an army camps against him and war rises against him, he will still be confident. The center of the psalm is verse 4. The one thing David asks is to dwell in the house of the Lord and behold his beauty. Fear loses its grip because his deepest desire is God himself.

The sections below look at how a psalm setting like this serves a congregation.

## What this song does in a room

Think of a congregation in a hard season. The plant in town is laying people off. A family is in a custody fight. A young woman is the only believer at her job and feels it every day. None of these is a battlefield in the literal sense, and each still feels like war to the people living it.

A sung psalm gives those people words they did not have to invent. There is weight in singing Scripture itself; the congregation is praying a prayer God's people have prayed for about three thousand years. That carries an authority a new lyric cannot.

For anxious people, the song offers more than an instruction not to be afraid. It gives a reason. David's courage comes from looking at God, and the song lets a room look in the same direction. Over time, a congregation that sings psalms also learns them, and the words come back on a sleepless night.

## What this song is saying about God

Psalm 27 makes three claims about God. He is light, showing the way when a person cannot see it. He is salvation, rescuing his people. He is the strength of life, a stronghold to run into. Each title answers a particular fear.

The psalm grounds confidence in God's presence, not in the absence of threat. David does not pretend his enemies are imaginary. He names them, then turns to the house of the Lord, where God hides him in the day of trouble and sets him on a rock. Worship sits at the center of the psalm's safety. What David wants most is to be near God.

The war language needs a careful frame. In the psalm, the enemies are David's own adversaries, from false witnesses to a hostile army. Christians read that language through Ephesians 6:12, which says our struggle is not against flesh and blood. Keep the song away from political or national enemies and let it serve its purpose: trust in God under pressure.

## Scriptural backbone

Psalm 27:1 opens the song's world: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Verse 3 gives the title its setting: "Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident."

Verse 4 is the heart: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD." Verse 5 adds the refuge: "in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion." The psalm closes in verse 14 with "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage." Romans 8:31 carries the same confidence into the New Testament: "If God be for us, who can be against us?" Read the whole psalm aloud before the song if you can; it takes about two minutes.

## How to use it in a service

Use it in a sermon series on the Psalms, or whenever Psalm 27 is the preaching text. It also serves well in seasons of crisis: after a tragedy, during a church conflict, or when your congregation is praying for persecuted believers elsewhere.

Consider pairing it with "In The Land Of The Living" so the room sings through more of the psalm's movement toward prayer and waiting. If you use only this song, read verses 7-14 aloud after it.

It also suits prayer services, commissioning moments and services of lament, where people need courage more than celebration.

Avoid attaching it to patriotic or military observances. The psalm is about trust in God, and its war language can be misheard in those settings.

## Things to watch for as the worship leader

Watch the translation. The words come from Scripture, and people who know Psalm 27 in another translation may notice differences. A quick note that the song follows the psalm closely invites them to listen for the text.

Watch the newness. Scripture songs can be wordier than typical choruses, so give the room a few weeks. Consider having a vocalist sing it first as a reading before you invite the congregation in.

Watch the person who is afraid. Do not scold fear. David admits the threat before he declares trust, and your words can do the same.

Check the range with a few untrained voices, and decide on your repeats before Sunday.

## A note for the team behind you (techs, vocalists, band)

Keep the words in front. Keys and guitar players, consider simple voicings that support the melody without crowding it. Drummers, try building gradually and saving the full kit for the strongest declarations of confidence, so the dynamics follow the psalm.

Vocalists, clear diction matters more than ornament, because every line is Scripture. Consider a single voice for the first pass and harmonies later. Techs, keep the lead vocal intelligible above the band, and put the psalm reference on the opening slide so people can find the passage in their own Bibles afterward.
